results.question: One of the purposes of "usable floor space" in building plan submissions is for determining:
results.responseText:

The Fire Safety Code defines **“usable floor area”** as the aggregate floor area excluding items such as staircases, public circulation space, lift landings, lavatories, WCs, kitchens in flats, and plant/service spaces [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 3 – Definitions]. It then states in **Clause B4.1** that **Table B1 should be used as the basis for calculating the occupant capacity** of a building or part of a building, and the table expressly uses **“occupancy factor (usable floor area in m² per person)”** for many uses [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2, Clause B4.1]. Evaluating each option: **A** is not supported by the retrieved text; PNAP APP-35 refers instead to **total usable floor space (TUFS)** for refuse storage/recycling provisions, not “usable floor space” as a general purpose for determining refuse chamber area [PNAP APP-35 (BD), Rev. 12/2022, Appendix C]. **B** is not supported by the retrieved context. **C** is incorrect because the definition is broader than “area within a flat” and is used for fire/occupant calculations, not simply to describe flat area [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 3 – Definitions]. **D** matches the code exactly: usable floor area is used to determine occupant capacity for evacuation [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2, Clause B4.1].

results.question: Which of the following is exempted from the provisions of the Buildings Ordinance?
results.responseText:
Under the Buildings Ordinance, **government buildings are exempted from the provisions of the Ordinance**, whereas ordinary private buildings are not. The retrieved context supports that the BO regulates building works and street works generally, including minor works [PNRC 73 (BD), current, p.1], and the Minor Works guidelines indicate that only specified categories are exempted, not all non-structural works [General Guidelines on Minor Works Control System (BD), current, p.1; p.4–5]. Per general HK regulatory practice, the Buildings Ordinance does **not** apply to buildings upon Government land and certain Government works, which is the basis for option C.

Evaluating each option:  
**A. Any street works** — incorrect. Street works are expressly treated as works subject to regulatory control rather than exempt in general [PNRC 73 (BD), current, p.1].  
**B. Any non-structural works** — incorrect. Non-structural works are not automatically exempt; some may be exempted building works or minor works, but not all [General Guidelines on Minor Works Control System (BD), current, p.4–5].  
**C. Works for any building belonging to the Government** — correct, per general HK regulatory practice under the Buildings Ordinance exemption for Government buildings/works.  
**D. Works for any building belonging to the Housing Society** — incorrect. Housing Society buildings are not generally exempt merely because of ownership.

The answer is C

This makes **D** the only option that is always required, per general HK regulatory practice (no retrieved clause text was provided here).

- **C. Lands Department approval under “design, disposition and height” clause** — this may be relevant under lease conditions for some sites, but it is not the universal statutory requirement triggered by CDA zoning itself.  
- **D. Approval by the Town Planning Board under Section 16 of the Town Planning Ordinance** — this is the defining approval mechanism for CDA development proposals, per general HK planning practice.

results.question: Who is the Licensing Authority for a restaurant situated at a licensed hotel?

The Fire Safety Code Annex also lists **“A Guide to Application for Restaurant Licences”** as issued by FEHD [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Annex A / Section 10 References]. A restaurant being **situated at a licensed hotel** does not change the restaurant licensing authority; hotel licensing is a separate regime.

**B. Commissioner of Police** — Incorrect. The retrieved Fire Safety Code shows Police-related licensing applies to matters such as massage establishments, not restaurant licences [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Annex A / Section 10 References].  
**C. Secretary for Home Affairs** — Incorrect. Home Affairs Department is associated with hotel/guesthouse and club-related guides in the Annex, not restaurant licences [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Annex A / Section 10 References].  
**D. Director of Food and Environmental Hygiene** — Correct, because FEHD is the authority issuing restaurant licences [Building Maintenance Guidebook (BD), current, Section 3 > 5.2.6 FEHD].

results.question:
Which combination of the following criteria requires a room to be provided with at least 2 exit doors?
(1) The size of the room exceeds 30 m2
(2) The capacity of the room exceeds 30 persons.
(3) The direct distance is below 18m but exceeds 15m.
(4) The travel distance is below 18m but exceeds 15m.
results.responseText:
Under the Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings, the minimum number of exit doors from a room is determined primarily by **occupant capacity**. A room with **4–30 persons** requires **1 exit door**, while a room with **31–200 persons** requires **2 exit doors** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Table B2; Clause B7.1]. Therefore, criterion **(2) the capacity of the room exceeds 30 persons** does require at least 2 exit doors.

Criterion **(1) room size exceeds 30 m²** is **not** shown in the retrieved provisions as a trigger for 2 exit doors. Criteria **(3) direct distance below 18m but exceeds 15m** and **(4) travel distance below 18m but exceeds 15m** are not supported by the retrieved text as triggers for requiring 2 exit doors; the retrieved clauses on exit-door numbers rely on occupant capacity, and where 2 or more exits are required, their arrangement must satisfy angle/separation rules [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clauses B11.6–B11.7]. Per general HK regulatory practice, travel distance affects means of escape acceptability, but the wording here does not make (3) or (4) the criterion that independently requires 2 exit doors.

Evaluating the options:  
- **A**: includes (1), which is not a trigger → incorrect.  
- **B**: includes (1) and (4); (1) is not a trigger → incorrect.  
- **C**: includes (2), which is the only supported trigger among the listed items; this is the best match.  
- **D**: relies only on (3) and (4), not supported → incorrect.  

**The answer is C**

results.question:
Irrespective of its distance from adjoining buildings, the roof
(1) of a domestic building must have an FRP of not less than 1 hour.
(2) of a single-staircase building of more than 13m above ground level should have an FRP of not less than 1 hour.
(3) of a building intended for use as a refuge floor must have an FRP of not less than 2 hours.
results.responseText:
(1) is **not supported** by the retrieved fire code text. The Code requires roofs generally to be constructed of non-combustible materials, but it does **not** state that every domestic building roof must have an FRR/FRP of at least 1 hour irrespective of separation distance [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C12.1]. The only retrieved roof FRR rules tied to specific situations are for single-staircase buildings over 13 m and roofs used as refuge floors [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clauses C12.2, C12.3]. So statement (1) is false on the provided sources.

(2) is **correct**: “The roof of every building with only one required staircase… in which the level of the highest floor is more than 13m above ground level should have an FRR of not less than that of the storey below” [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C12.2]. Since the storey below in such cases would require at least 1 hour fire resistance per general HK fire-resisting construction tables/practice, this supports the 1-hour proposition, though the clause itself is framed as “not less than that of the storey below.”

(3) is **correct**: “The main roof or any other part of the roof, which is used or intended to be used as a refuge floor or part of a refuge floor, should have an FRR of not less than that of the storey below” [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C12.3; see also PNAP APP-153 (BD), current, Item 17 amending C12.3]. Under general HK regulatory practice, refuge floors require 2-hour fire resistance, so the statement is consistent.

**The answer is C**

- **C (2) and (3) only)**: incomplete, because **purpose-built department store (4)** is also included.

Evaluating the options:  
- **A (1) and (2) only)**: consistent with C3.1 (control of fire spread) and C4 (containment/minimisation of smoke spread).  
- **B (1) and (3) only)**: (1) is correct, but (3) is not the direct purpose of compartmentation itself; orderly evacuation is a broader fire safety objective, not the specific concept of compartmentation.  
- **C (2) and (4) only)**: (2) is supportable, but (4) has no basis in the regulations.

results.question:

Per general HK regulatory practice, such internal private streets used for site classification are treated as requiring EVA compliance.

(3) **Windows may face it as external air** — per general HK regulatory practice, a private street created within a site for site classification can be treated as a street for purposes of lighting and ventilation, so windows may face it as external air, subject to the applicable regulations and dimensions. This point is not covered in the retrieved EVA texts, so this conclusion is based on general HK practice rather than the retrieved sources.  

(4) **Area not counted for site area calculation** — this is **not correct** as a general statement. Per general HK regulatory practice, the area of a private street within the site is not automatically excluded from site area calculation merely because it is created for site classification.

Evaluating the options:  
- **A (1) and (2) only)**: incorrect because (1) is not necessarily required.

results.question: Which of the following building uses does not require risers and treads to be respectively less than 175 mm and greater than 225 mm for Means of Escape staircases?
results.responseText:
For **cinema complex (A)**, the retrieved text gives a stricter stair requirement for places of public entertainment under Section 3: required staircases must have **treads not less than 280 mm** and **risers not more than 150 mm** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause B23.1]. So a cinema complex clearly **does require** dimensions tighter than 175/225.

For **kindergarten (C)** and **hospital (D)**, although the retrieved extracts do not show the exact clause, under general HK regulatory practice these are sensitive occupancies and their means of escape staircases are subject to the usual requirement of **risers less than 175 mm and treads greater than 225 mm** (or stricter), not an exemption. The heritage guidebook also indicates BD treats facilities serving children, elderly and low-mobility persons more stringently, not more leniently [Practice Guidebook for Heritage Buildings 2012 (2021 Edition) (BD), 2012 (2021 Edition), §5.16].  

That leaves **primary school (B)** as the use that **does not require** the 175 mm / 225 mm criterion for MOE staircases; schools are generally dealt with under a different stair geometry standard in the fire safety code, whereas cinema/hospital/kindergarten are not exempt on that basis. This part is based on **general HK regulatory practice**, as the exact school clause is not in the retrieved text. **Version caveat:** the cited fire safety code is the **2011 (2024 Edition)**, and users should confirm no later amendment applies.

**The answer is B**

results.question: Under the Building (Demolition Works) Regulations, which of the following is not necessary for the Authorized Person appointed in respect of the demolition works to carry out before commencement of the demolition works?
results.responseText:
Before demolition starts, the AP must liaise with utility companies, keep records of utilities, and cause all utilities to be terminated; the demolition plan must also ensure existing utilities in the vicinity are not affected [Code of Practice for Demolition of Buildings (BD), 2004, Section 2.1.3]. The HA General Specification likewise requires existing services to be identified and all statutory authority installations to be safely disconnected and associated fittings/equipment removed before commencement [General Specification for Building Works (HA), 2024 Edition, DEM.D120.1]. The BD Code is a cross-reference document under the demolition regulatory framework [Code of Practice for Demolition of Buildings (BD), 2004, Appendix D].

Evaluating the options: **B** is necessary because gas and electricity supplies are utilities that must be terminated [BD COP 2004, Section 2.1.3]. **D** is also necessary in substance, because associated fittings/equipment relating to disconnected statutory installations are to be removed [HA GS 2024, DEM.D120.1; per general HK regulatory practice this aligns with pre-demolition utility isolation/removal requirements]. **C** is necessary if such tramway or street-lighting fittings attached to the building are affected, as statutory/utility installations in the vicinity must be identified, consulted on, and protected/removed as appropriate [BD COP 2004, Section 2.1.1(B), 2.1.3]. **A** is the one not identified in the retrieved demolition-regulation requirements as a mandatory pre-commencement duty of the AP under the utility/disconnection provisions.

The answer is A

results.question: Which elements must satisfy stability, integrity, and insulation under FRC Code?
results.responseText:
Under Table C2 of the Fire Safety Code, a **structural frame, beam or column** requires **stability only** (Y/N/N), so **A is not correct** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Table C2]. A **non-loadbearing wall being a fire barrier** requires **integrity and insulation only** (N/Y/Y), so **B is not correct** if “compartment wall” is taken as a non-loadbearing fire barrier [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Table C2].

An **enclosure around services in required staircase/protected lobby** requires **integrity and insulation only** (N/Y/Y), so **C is not correct** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Table C2, Item 14]. A **protected shaft, lobby and corridor** requires **stability, integrity and insulation** where loadbearing is involved (Y*/Y/Y), and a lift shaft is treated under the Code as a protected shaft/lift protection provision; therefore **D is the only option that matches stability, integrity and insulation** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Table C2, Item 8; Clause C9.3]. Version caveat: citations are from the 2011 Code, 2024 Edition; PNAP APP-153 confirms Table C2 governs the applicable criteria and exposure method [PNAP APP-153: Fire Safety Code 2011 (BD), current, Clause C4.2].

The answer is D

results.question: Which is NOT required for a bridge uniting two buildings without fire shutters/lobbies under FRC Code?

The commentary adds that where no fire barriers are provided, the bridge should be an unenclosed bridge of non-combustible materials to prevent fire spread and allow smoke dispersal [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Commentary to Clause C15.1].
